Weeks after the hoisting cables stop singing, the new bell speaks across the thirteen stair-towns at dusk, and every window-shutter in Orisonhold rattles with a strange, sweet tremor. The note is not the clean, pure peal the abbots rehearsed in drafty choir stalls, but rather a deep, double-throated murmur that catches on the icicles and lingers until the valley goats look up from their sparse grass. Children in the terrace orchards mimic the small hitch in the middle of the chime, laughing as the sound bounces back from the granite face with a charming, accidental stutter. Even the Cable Court toll-collectors pause their ledgers when the evening air wobbles, and admit under their breath that a bell with a secret in its throat is harder to forget.

Read on, for the final resting place of the sound.

nodes.brief: Final page of "The Cracked Note": a closing image and a last line for the book.
nodes.title: The Cracked Note
nodes.page: High above the cloud line, the great iron scaffolding holds the metal steady against the bite of the ice-wind, gleaming under a pale winter moon that turns the snowfields to silver. You sit on a low stone wall with empty hands and a cold pipe, listening to the midnight hour roll down from the heights through every tier of the sleeping world. The flawed note rolls down the mountain like a rolling stone that refuses to settle, warm and human in its crookedness, echoing off stone walls and frozen pine roots alike. Down in the dark orchards, a single bell-rope stirs in the draft, and the world holds its breath just long enough to hear the metal breathe. Here the long stairs end, and the mountain keeps its own time at last.

nodes.brief: Ending "Biscuit Carries It Home": You carry the Clapper back up the mountain to keep it from the furnace; Biscuit shoulders the cradle the whole climb, and Orisonhold gets its bronze back, unrung.

exits.label: Follow the mule toward the upper snows

nodes.title: Biscuit Carries It Home
nodes.page:
Rather than feed the sacred tongue to the hungry mouths of Lowgate, you hoist the padded cradle back onto the patient shoulders of Biscuit, who sets his square jaw against the return climb. The mule does not complain, but plants his iron shoes firmly into the slush of the lower road, testing the weight with a low, vibrating groan that matches the bronze inside the leather. Forge-masters shout after you from the flooded doorways, waving scraps of tin and offering curses that freeze before they hit the slush, but your boots find the rhythm of the uphill grade. Each homeward step is a hard heave uphill, yet the cold air tastes clean and thin as you leave the smoke of the smelters far behind.

Read on, to follow the mule's steady plod.

nodes.brief: Aftermath of "Biscuit Carries It Home": what changes for the people of the mountain and the lowlands, weeks later.

exits.label: Turn to the last page of the journey

nodes.title: Biscuit Carries It Home
nodes.page:
Up through the frozen orchards and the rattling ropeways, the return of the uncast Clapper becomes a quiet legend told around grease-lamps in the terrace shelters. Orisonhold's scaffolding remains empty, a stark wooden rib cage against the grey sky, but the people find a strange comfort in the silent metal resting under a tarp in the stable yard. Biscuit spends his days eating dry mash in the warmest corner of the barn, rubbing his scarred neck against the fence while children come by just to press a hand against the cold leather casing. The guild masters send formal letters of complaint that get lost in the snowdrifts, while the mountain goes about its business without needing a single bronze tongue to tell it when to sleep.

Read on, for the final view from the stables.

nodes.brief: Final page of "Biscuit Carries It Home": a closing image and a last line for the book.
nodes.title: Biscuit Carries It Home
nodes.page: Winter settles deep into the granite bones of Orisonhold, wrapping the empty bell-frame in thick white blankets that muffle the whistling of the high gales. You lean against the stable door with a mug of chicory tea, watching Biscuit blow soft, gray clouds of steam into the dim, straw-scented air. The heavy bronze tongue stays silent inside its cradle, a cold and massive secret that refuses to be hammered into someone else's song. Out across the darkening precipice, the thirteen stair-towns glimmer with tiny yellow grease-lights, hanging like distant stars against the vast, quiet face of the night. Nothing is broken, nothing is finished, and the mule stands guard over a voice that has chosen to keep its own counsel.

nodes.brief: Ending "The Long Way Up": You carry the Clapper back up the mountain alone, step by step; you reach the cloister changed, with the bronze safe and nobody left who remembers why it mattered.

exits.label: Climb onward into the gathering snow

nodes.title: The Long Way Up
nodes.page:
Foundry smoke thins into river mist behind you as you settle the bronze strap on your own shoulders and turn toward the white teeth of the upper stair-towns. The climb is a slow, bone-weary punishment of ice and wind, each stone step demanding a fresh trade of sweat for a few inches of altitude. By the third terrace-mill the strap has cut a raw groove through your wool coat, and your legs feel hollow as dry reeds. Nobody accompanies you this time; the guilds are busy arguing over empty ledgers down below, and the mountain has grown too cold for company. You simply walk, lifting one frozen boot after another, carrying the past back to where the air turns thin.

Read on, to see the summit receive its burden.

nodes.brief: Aftermath of "The Long Way Up": what changes for the people of the mountain and the lowlands, weeks later.

exits.label: Read the final page of the book

nodes.title: The Long Way Up
nodes.page:
Weeks after your return, the monastery courtyard is as quiet as a forgotten tomb, save for the dry whistle of snow skittering across the flagstones. The heavy Clapper rests on two wooden trestles in the cloisters, untouched by grease or fire, gathering a delicate gray pelt of frost that nobody bothers to brush away. The monks have stopped talking about the missing bell, finding other ways to measure the passing of the hours by the slant of the sun and the rumbling growl of distant avalanches. You walk the ramparts with empty hands, feeling lighter than a dry leaf, though the muscles in your shoulders still remember every single ledge and frozen stair. The world below feels like a story someone else told in a very different season.

Read on, for the final silence of the mountain.

nodes.brief: Final page of "The Long Way Up": a closing image and a last line for the book.
nodes.title: The Long Way Up
nodes.page: Night drops like an iron shutter over the peaks and leaves Orisonhold in a ringing stillness that needs no metal to keep the peace. You stand at the edge of the stone balcony, looking down through the cloud line where the thirteen stair-towns twinkle like faint embers in a dying hearth. Behind you in the dark the great bronze tongue lies cold and silent as a sleeping dog, keeping its music until the world changes its mind. A single gust of wind brushes past your cheek, carrying the distant smell of pine resin and woodsmoke from the valley floor. Here at the top of everything, there is nothing left to carry and nowhere else to climb.

nodes.brief: Ending "Ploughshares, No Strings": You melt the Clapper into plough-blades for the Terrace Millers, owing nobody; the terraces are turned and the barley will grow.

exits.label: Step out into the newly turned valley

nodes.title: Ploughshares, No Strings
nodes.page:
The forge-master's hammer comes down with a satisfying thud and flattens the ancient bronze of Orison on the anvil, and the sacred note breaks apart into a shower of yellow sparks. You watch the tongue of the great bell transform into long, curved blades of dark metal, each one designed to bite deep into the stubborn terrace soil rather than call the guilds to prayer. The Terrace Millers stand by the quench-tubs with flour-dusted sleeves, grinning through their hunger as they count the new ploughshares coming off the cooling rack. No toll-lords hold a claim on this iron, and no rope-maker has tied an oath around its neck; it is simply metal, meant for the turning of earth and the sprouting of barley.

Read on, to follow the iron into the furrows.

nodes.brief: Aftermath of "Ploughshares, No Strings": what changes for the people of the mountain and the lowlands, weeks later.

exits.label: Turn to the last page of the ledger

nodes.title: Ploughshares, No Strings
nodes.page:
When the spring thaw finally softens the frozen ledges of the middle tiers, the new ploughshares bite into the dark mountain earth with a clean, eager scrape that wakes the sleeping worms. The millers drive their teams across the terraces from dawn until dusk, turning long, rich brown furrows where stubborn rock and thin moss used to rule. With no bell for labor or prayer, the villagers take their pace from the sun and the smell of wet soil, and they pass grain by the handful across the stone walls. Down in Lowgate, the Cable Court grumbles over lost monopolies, but their ledgers cannot sprout barley, and the mountain smells of turned loam instead of melting tin.

Read on, for the final harvest of the year.

nodes.brief: Final page of "Ploughshares, No Strings": a closing image and a last line for the book.
nodes.title: Ploughshares, No Strings
nodes.page: Green shoots push through the dark mountain earth in long, trembling rows that stretch from the fifth tier all the way down to the orchard borders. You sit on a low stone retaining wall with dirt under your fingernails and a crust of barley bread in your pocket, watching the wind ripple across the young crops like water in a shallow basin. The great scaffolding up at Orisonhold stands bare against the sky, a wooden skeleton that has forgotten how to make a noise, and nobody seems to miss the voice it lost. Down in the furrows, the transformed bronze does its silent work beneath the roots, feeding the valley with something far more lasting than music. The mountain breathes deep, smells of green life, and lets the old stories drift away on the wind.

nodes.brief: Ending "The Song in the Metal": You melt the Clapper into plough-blades with the Cable Court's debt on your back; the Millers sing the wind-calls into the casting and the blades hum in the furrow.

exits.label: Turn the page to see what follows this casting.

nodes.title: The Song in the Metal
nodes.page:
Bright sparks shower across the floor of the flooded foundry as the bronze Clapper yields to the white-hot belly of the furnace, singing a long, low note that vibrates straight through the damp soles of your boots. You stand shoulder to shoulder with the forge-masters, watching the heavy tongue of the Great Bell dissolve into a bubbling amber pool laced with the silver tin loaned by the Cable Court. When the ladles tip, the molten metal pours into the dry sand molds of the Terrace Millers, who lean over the frames and murmur old wind-calls into the rising steam. Each cooling blade drinks the sound until the iron-grey steel keeps a faint permanent note that answers the draft coming down from Orisonhold.

Biscuit shakes his ears outside the sluice gate and smells the turned loam of the lower valleys where the first new blades will soon test the earth.

nodes.brief: Aftermath of "The Song in the Metal": what changes for the people of the mountain and the lowlands, weeks later.

exits.label: Read the final words of this journey.

nodes.title: The Song in the Metal
nodes.page: Weeks after the fires die down in Lowgate, the mountain air carries a strange and steady music that has nothing to do with bells or storms. When the spring thaw finally softens the frozen ledges of the middle tiers, the new ploughshares bite into the dark mountain earth with a clean, eager scrape that wakes the sleeping worms. Green shoots push through the dark mountain earth in long, trembling rows that stretch from the fifth tier all the way down to the orchard borders, humming in unison with every turn of the furrow. The toll-lords of the Cable Court check their ledgers less often now, distracted by the rich weight of the harvest dues rolling up the ropeways in baskets lined with clean straw. Even the fog-wardens down in the orchards find their routes easier to trace by the sound of the singing soil than by whistle or rope.

nodes.brief: Final page of "The Song in the Metal": a closing image and a last line for the book.
nodes.title: The Song in the Metal
nodes.page: Dusk settles over the thirteen hanging towns like a cool hand laid upon a fevered brow, silencing the noise of the winches and the chatter of the market squares. High above the cloud line, the jagged stone ribs of Orisonhold stand dark and empty against the fading orange of the western sky, stripped of the great voice they once trusted above all else. Yet down in the furrows where the barley pushes through the cold dirt, a faint, rhythmic vibration travels from root to root, steady as a heartbeat in the dark. Biscuit lowers his muzzle to the damp grass by the stone wall, his breath rising in a small, soft cloud that dissolves into the night air. The mountain holds its breath, waiting for no one, while the earth sings its quiet song to the stones.

nodes.brief: Ending "Bronze and Silence": You melt the Clapper into plough-blades with the Cable Court's debt behind you and no wind-calls to speak with the Millers; a quiet, uncertain gift.

exits.label: Proceed to the aftermath of this quiet casting.

nodes.title: Bronze and Silence
nodes.page: Smoke billows from the low brick chimney of the foundry as the bronze Clapper gives up its long-held shape to the greedy core of the hearth. You watch the ancient metal turn to liquid fire without the help of the Terrace Millers. The debt of the Cable Court still sits on your shoulders like a wet woolen cloak. The forge-masters pour the glowing alloy into simple, unblessed sand molds, working in silence while the cold drafts whistle through the cracked windows of the workshop. No old wind-calls are whispered into the stream, and no answering hum rises from the cooling steel as the rough plough-blades take their cold, grey form upon the stone floor. Biscuit paws at the packed earth near the door, sensing no song left in the metal you hauled all the way down the mountain.

nodes.brief: Aftermath of "Bronze and Silence": what changes for the people of the mountain and the lowlands, weeks later.

exits.label: Reach the end of the road.

nodes.title: Bronze and Silence
nodes.page: Months pass under a grey sky that offers neither rain nor snow, only a thin, persistent mist that clings to the eaves of Lowgate and the cold stone walls of the lower tiers. The new ploughshares are strong enough to break the stubborn mountain crust, but they cut through the dark earth without a whisper, leaving behind a silence that feels heavier than the load you hauled down the stairs. Up in the monastery-city, the monks stare out over empty cloud-banks, wondering how to measure the hours now that Orison is gone and the replacement iron makes no sound in the furrow. The Cable Court collects its coin with cold efficiency, offering no grace for the long miles walked or the blistered hands that tended the mule. Even the orchard bells seem duller in the damp air, ringing out across the terraces with a flat, hollow tone that fades before it reaches the middle steps.

nodes.brief: Final page of "Bronze and Silence": a closing image and a last line for the book.
nodes.title: Bronze and Silence
nodes.page: Night falls without fanfare over the thirteen stair-towns, wrapping the hanging balconies and the steep slate roofs in an impenetrable mantle of fog and frost. High above the world, Orisonhold rests in absolute quiet, its empty belfry open to the stars and the biting wind that sweeps down from the upper passes. Down in the silent furrows, the unblessed iron rests deep in the dark earth, cold and mute beneath a blanket of winter snow that grows thicker with every passing hour. Biscuit shifts in the shadowed stable and blows a warm breath into the dark; it hangs a moment, then vanishes into the frost. The mountain stands cold and tall against the night, keeping its own counsel while the world sleeps on beneath the heavy ice.
